title: Drude SILCS-Nucleic: harnessing explicit electronic polarization in targeting RNA and DNA for drug design.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the Europe PMC supplement (27.9 MB zip: one 25.5 MB PDF plus figure images) and extracted the PDF text myself. Confirmed the supplement holds Tables S1-S10 as PDF text only: S8 = SILCS-MC Ligand Grid Free Energy (a simulation score), ligand efficiency and pose RMSD (root-mean-square deviation from the experimental pose) for up to 9 poses per ligand; S9 = Glide docking score and MM-GBSA energy; S10 = Gnina predicted affinity. Counted the study's scope from Tables S5-S7: 6 nucleic acid targets (DDX, TGQ, TAR, HCV, IVP, GUA) and 7 target-ligand pairs (IVP-DPQ, TAR-RBT203, TAR-RRM, TAR-NEOB, GUA-dGua, HCV-Benz, TGQ-MM41). Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.21873007 responds (HTTP 200, redirects to record 21873008) but neither its web page nor its application programming interface returned any content here, so I could not list its files.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the Zenodo deposit and GitHub repository (hmmichel/drude_silcs_nucleic) contain code only - the data availability statement says 'all code necessary to reproduce the findings'; I could not open either to confirm. Simulation details (microseconds of Grand Canonical Monte Carlo / molecular dynamics per system, ~120-200 nanoseconds per day throughput) are from the methods text.

a1_downloadable.note: The only machine-readable artefact is a 25.5 MB PDF of figures and tables; no numeric data file exists. The Zenodo deposit is described as code, and I could not enumerate its contents (page and API returned nothing), so no feature/label table is downloadable.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Nothing is a column: every number sits inside PDF tables I had to re-extract from compressed PDF streams. A prediction target (measured binding affinity for these ligands) appears nowhere in the supplement; it would have to be constructed from the primary literature cited per system.

a3_inputs_present.note: Ligands appear as nicknames (DPQ, RBT203, NEOB, MM41, dGua, Benz) with no SMILES strings; targets appear as 6 Protein Data Bank codes (1ZHU, 3UYH, 6CMN, 2LWK, 3SKI, 1QD3). Structures and chemical structures both need outside lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated in every table caption I read: kcal/mol for grid free energies and docking scores, kcal/mol per atom for ligand efficiency, angstroms for pose RMSD.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified in Tables S5-S10: 6 nucleic acid targets and 7 target-ligand pairs. Counting each docked pose separately gives roughly 378 rows (7 pairs x up to 9 poses x 2 force fields x 3 programs), but poses of the same ligand are not independent examples. Far below the ~1,500-row bar.

a6_fits_laptop.note: The published artefacts are tiny; however, regenerating FragMaps (3D grids of fragment binding free energy) is supercomputer work - the paper used the Expanse cluster at ~120-200 nanoseconds per day per system.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Six systems in the methods text match the six columns of Table S3 and the ligand lists in Tables S6-S7; no count conflicts found.

a8_label_provenance.note: Every numeric value is another program's output: Ligand Grid Free Energy from SILCS (Site Identification by Ligand Competitive Saturation) simulations, GlideScore and MM-GBSA from Schrodinger, predicted affinity from Gnina (itself a neural network). Training on these distils force fields, not biology. The only measured quantities are the 6-7 experimental structures, and pose RMSD is computed against them from the method's own output.

existing_models.name: Drude SILCS-Nucleic (this paper's own method; physics-based, not machine learning)
existing_models.score_and_split: Mean pose RMSD (root-mean-square deviation from the experimental pose) 1.9-3.0 angstroms for groove binders with Drude FragMaps versus 2.1-3.9 angstroms with the CHARMM36 force field, on 7 target-ligand pairs with known structures; no held-out split exists because nothing is trained.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Their discussion states that 'no current approach fully addresses the challenges of modeling nucleic acid-small molecule interactions' and calls for benchmarking across more diverse nucleic acid motifs and ligand classes.

existing_models.name: RNAmigos2 (graph neural network for structure-based RNA virtual screening, Nature Communications 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported by its authors to rival docking accuracy while screening about 10,000x faster, with in vitro confirmation of hits; I read the search result summary, not the paper, so I did not verify its numbers or split.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not checked - I did not retrieve the full paper.

existing_models.name: SMRTnet (multimodal deep learning for small molecule-RNA interaction, Nature Biotechnology 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Described by its authors as substantially outperforming existing tools across several experimental benchmarks without needing RNA tertiary structures; numbers and split not verified by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not checked - I did not retrieve the full paper.

existing_models.name: DeepMIF and EMMPTNet (deep learning RNA-small molecule affinity predictors, 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: DeepMIF reports Pearson correlation 0.796 on a benchmark of 1,439 RNA-small molecule pairs; EMMPTNet reports Pearson 0.773. Taken from search-result summaries, not from the papers themselves.

backbone.name: RNA-FM (RNA language model) or an equivariant graph network on nucleic acid structures
backbone.hardware: Irrelevant here: with 7 labelled target-ligand pairs there is nothing to fit a head on.
backbone.licence: Not assessed - project stopped at Part A.

integration.partner_dataset: PDBbind / HARIBOSS (curated RNA-ligand complexes with measured affinities) joinable on Protein Data Bank identifier
integration.join_key: PDB ID, plus ligand chemical component identifier
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does explicit electronic polarization improve binding-pose and affinity prediction across the few hundred known RNA-ligand complexes, not just six? - but that question needs new simulations on a supercomputer, not this paper's released artefacts.

controls.positive_control: Recovery of the known binding sites in the six structures, which the paper already reports qualitatively.
controls.negative_control: Not applicable - no model would be trained.
controls.external_validation: HARIBOSS / PDBbind RNA-ligand subsets exist, but would require re-running the simulation pipeline rather than reusing released data.

honest_claim_h3: Nothing can be claimed from a model built on these files: the released artefacts describe how 7 ligand-target pairs scored under three scoring programs, so any model trained on them would be reporting the behaviour of a force field on six molecules.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use nucleic acid structure and ligand chemistry to predict where and how tightly a small molecule binds RNA or DNA.
plain_idea.train_on: What I considered: each example would be an RNA or DNA pocket plus a candidate small molecule. This paper supplies only 7 such pairs across 6 targets, which I counted in the supplementary tables.
plain_idea.predict: Binding pose accuracy and binding strength in kcal/mol. In this paper the 'answers' are themselves computed by simulation software (SILCS, Glide, Gnina); the only measured input is 6 experimental structures from X-ray crystallography or nuclear magnetic resonance.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: RNA-targeted drug discovery badly needs reliable scoring, and a model that ranked compounds well would redirect medicinal chemistry effort. But learning it requires hundreds to thousands of measured complexes, which this paper does not provide.

more_or_better_data.why: Seven target-ligand pairs here versus the 1,439-pair benchmark that DeepMIF reports using. This paper's contribution is a simulation protocol, not data volume.

confidence_score.why: Up to nine poses per ligand give a spread of scores, but that reflects sampling of one simulation, not independent measurement replicates, so it cannot calibrate prediction confidence.

models_beatable.why: The comparators are a 2025 polarizable force field workflow, Schrodinger Glide and Gnina 1.3 - physics and scoring tools, not a stale neural network with a weak split. Separately, RNA-ligand machine learning models from 2025 (SMRTnet, RNAmigos2, DeepMIF) already occupy the learned-scoring space.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: there is no trainable baseline to beat and no labelled table to extend, since the deposit is code and the numbers live in a PDF.

ml_idea: The only machine learning idea this paper supports would be learning to emulate SILCS FragMaps (3D grids of fragment binding free energy) so that polarizable-force-field scoring could be applied without supercomputer simulation. That is a legitimate idea, but it needs the FragMap grids for many systems as training data, and the released deposit is code only - six targets' worth of grids would not train anything.

effort.compute_note: Only the 28 MB supplement was handled, which cost seconds; no modelling workload was estimated because Part A failed. Generating comparable data from scratch needs cluster-scale molecular dynamics (the authors used the Expanse supercomputer at ~120-200 nanoseconds per day per system).
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the target-ligand pairs in the supplement: 7 across 6 targets. That one count kills it, and it took one PDF text extraction.

verdict_reason: A molecular simulation methods paper, not a dataset. Verified in the supplement: 6 nucleic acid targets, 7 target-ligand pairs, all numbers trapped in a 25 MB PDF, and every value is another program's output (SILCS grid free energy, GlideScore, Gnina affinity) rather than a measurement. That fails A5 (far under 1,500 rows), A8 (labels are model predictions), A1/A2/A3 (no machine-readable table, no target column, no SMILES or structures). The released Zenodo and GitHub artefacts are code for re-running the workflow, which I could not open from here but which the authors describe as code only.
